title: Designing a Predictive Talent Index Based on Your Best People
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article presents a sophisticated approach to talent selection: rather than relying on generic personality assessments or intuitive judgment, the best organizations use their own top performers as a data set to identify what personality patterns, styles, and preferences actually predict success in their specific culture and context. The process involves having the organization's best people complete multiple assessment instruments until a common pattern emerges — for example, all top performers scoring as High D and High C on DISC, or sharing a specific profile on the Big Five. Once that predictive pattern is confirmed, it can be used as a 'secret sauce' in future selection. The article acknowledges that identifying such a pattern is difficult and may take years of data collection across a large set of assessment tools, but argues the investment is worth it because it produces a genuinely predictive instrument rather than a generic one. The most important distinction the article makes is between using assessments as general predictors of personality type (how most organizations use them) versus using them as empirically-validated predictors of success in a specific organizational context (what the best organizations do).
points: The key innovation is empirical validation within the organization: instead of using generic assessment benchmarks, the best leaders map their actual top performers to find what patterns the assessments reveal about success in their specific culture.

The investment required is substantial — years of data collection, multiple assessment instruments across a large pool of top performers — but produces something no off-the-shelf assessment can: a genuinely organization-specific predictor.

Most organizations use personality assessments as general predictors of how someone will behave; the best organizations use them as predictors of how someone will perform specifically here, given our norms, values, and expectations.

Once confirmed, the predictive pattern functions as a 'mirror of success': it tells the organization not just who is likely to succeed but what success in their culture actually looks like in terms of personality and style.

The article's honest acknowledgment that finding such a pattern is 'exceedingly difficult' and may take 'several years' sets realistic expectations and implicitly critiques organizations that expect one assessment cycle to yield a predictive instrument.
quotes: To evaluate and select talent, organizations naturally rely on personality assessments and psychological diagnostics to learn more about people. By digging deeper into the motivations, tendencies, and styles of prospective candidates and those up for promotion, leaders gain the data and confidence they need to make better choices.

As general predictors of how people will show up and behave once in a position, these assessments add a lot of value, which is one reason they are so popular. Because good leaders treat assessment results as another data point and not as a litmus test for selection, it is not uncommon for organizations to use multiple diagnostics at the same time.

But the best leaders and organizations have learned to take the fullest advantage of these assessments by using them more strategically. Leaders naturally want a true predictive tool to make their selections more accurate, so they turn to their best people to create one.

Finding a common pattern of that success can be a huge advantage in the selection process. The best leaders ask their top people to complete as many diagnostics and assessments as possible until a pattern correlated with success emerges.

For example, if an organization relies on the DISC assessment to test for features of personality, applying this tool to the best performers may reveal a pattern that can be used for prediction. If nearly all the organization’s top performers share a common set of personality results (in DISC, let’s say they are all High Ds and Cs), that pattern can now be used to find others with the same orientation.

Organizations can spend several years with a large set of assessment tools before they land on a pattern they have confidence in. But once they concoct that magic potion, it can significantly improve their selection process.
Organizations that do the work end up with more than a predictive tool. They create a mirror of what success in personality and style actually looks like in their culture.
